Lay days, that is to say the period of waiting of the vessel for loading and discharging, shall commence, with respect to loading, on the day following that on which the charterer is notified of the readiness of the vessel to receive goods, and, with respect to discharging, on the day following that on which the consignee is enabled to begin discharging under the conditions provided for in the contract.

The commencement and duration of the period of waiting of the vessel shall vary according to the customs of the place if they are not fixed by the agreement. Only working days shall be included in the computation of the period of waiting.

Demurrage shall run ipso jure from the expiry of the period fixed in the contract for loading or for discharging. If the contract does not fix the number of lay days, demurrage shall not begin to run until twenty-four hours after the master has given written notice thereof to the charterer, the consignee or their representative.

All working days and non-working days shall be included in counting the days of demurrage. If the period of demurrage fixed in the agreement or according to the customs of the place expires, the master may claim for each additional day compensation equal to the amount due for each day of demurrage plus one-half of that amount.
The period of waiting shall be interrupted in the event of physical impossibility to load or discharge. Conversely, force majeure shall not interrupt the running of demurrage.
Compensation for demurrage and compensation due for additional days shall be deemed additional freight.

A contract of charter of a vessel or a contract of carriage shall be rescinded ipso jure and without compensation if, before any commencement of performance, force majeure supervenes and renders such performance wholly impossible. If force majeure supervenes before the departure of the vessel and after the commencement of performance of the contract, rescission shall be ordered subject to compensation if the case so requires.

If, however, the force majeure prevents the departure of the vessel only temporarily, the contract shall remain in force without any increase in freight or compensation, save that rescission shall take effect ipso jure if the delay results in the frustration of the commercial transaction for which the contracting parties or one of them entered into the contract of charter or of carriage.

The lessor of the vessel shall have a lien on the goods constituting the cargo to secure payment of the freight of his vessel and its accessories for a period of fifteen days after delivery of the goods, provided that they have not passed into the hands of a third party.

The lessor of the vessel shall have the right to retain the goods by reason of non-payment of their freight unless security is furnished to him, and he may also apply for them to be deposited in the hands of a third party up to the amount of the payment of the freight of the vessel and apply for their sale if they are perishable.

A contract of charter of a vessel and of carriage by sea shall be proved by written evidence; this instrument shall be called a charterparty or a bill of lading according to the nature of the carriage by sea, save that the contracting parties shall be exempted from drawing up a written instrument in the case of short-sea coasting trade from port to port.

The charter-party is the instrument that proves the chartering of the vessel. This instrument shall be drawn up in the form of an instrument under private signature executed in two original copies. It is required that the following be stated therein:

1) The names of the contracting parties.

2) The name of the vessel and its tonnage, unless it has been stipulated that "the vessel shall be designated subsequently".

3) The name of the master.

4) The goods required to be loaded, specified by their nature and quantity.

5) The freight (price of the voyage).

6) The time and place agreed upon for loading and discharge.

The bill of lading is an instrument for the loaded goods given by the master, and it is drawn up in three copies:

One copy for the shipper, a second for the consignee, and a third for the master.

It is required that the following be stated therein:

1) The names of the contracting parties: the shipowner and the charterer.

2) Specification of the loaded goods by their nature, weight, volume, and marks (brands)

3) The name of the vessel and its nationality.

4) The conditions of carriage, including the freight of the vessel, the place of departure, and the place of destination

5) The date of delivery of the bill of lading

6) The number of copies drawn up by the master

7) The signature of the master and the shipper.
Any copy of the copies of the bill of lading that omits the mention of the matters set forth above shall only avail as prima facie evidence.

The mention of the marks (brands) of the packages, their number, and the quantity, nature, and weight of the goods shall be made on the basis of the written particulars submitted by the shipper prior to loading.

The marks must be sufficient to identify the goods and must be affixed in such a manner that they always remain easily legible until the end of the voyage. The carrier may refuse to enter the declarations of the shipper in the bill of lading if he has reasonable grounds for suspecting their accuracy or if he has not had the ordinary means of checking them.

In this case, he must state the grounds and this liability. Thereupon, the proof of shortage falls upon the sender or the receiver. The document given to the shipper prior to the loading of his goods shall be exchanged, after such loading and at his request, for a regular bill of lading.

The bill of lading given in the form prescribed above proves, unless contrary evidence is adduced, the receipt by the carrier of the goods as described in the bill of lading.

If the declaration of the shipper regarding the marks of the goods, or their number, quantity, nature, or weight is contrary to the truth, he shall be held liable towards the carrier for all damages resulting from his declaration, but the carrier may not invoke this untrue declaration against any person whomsoever other than the shipper.

A bill of lading shall be either to a named person, or to order, or to bearer. A bill of lading to a named person is non-negotiable, and the master may not deliver the goods except to the person named therein.

A bill of lading to order is negotiable by endorsement, which must be dated. The master may not deliver the goods except to the holder of the endorsed bill of lading, even if endorsed in blank.

A bill of lading to bearer is negotiable by mere delivery. The master must deliver the goods to any person who presents himself with this bill of lading.

Copies of a bill of lading drawn up to order or to bearer must contain the mention of this phrase: "negotiable" or this phrase: "non-negotiable", and an indication of the number of copies and the stipulation that the remaining copies shall be void in the event that one of them is used.

The carrier may not set up against the holder of a negotiable and endorsed copy the defences that may be raised against the shipper, unless he proves that the holder of this copy is acting as an agent for the shipper. The guarantee of the endorser, which is without joint and several liability, extends only to the existence of the shipped goods and the validity of the contract of carriage.

If, prior to the delivery of any goods by the master, a dispute arises between the holders of various copies of the same negotiable bill of lading, the copy bearing the earliest endorsement shall have preference over the others.

However, after the goods have been received by the holder of one of the negotiable copies, the holder of another copy may not be preferred over him, even if the latter bears an earlier date.

If there is a discrepancy between the bill of lading containing the signature of the shipper and the bills of lading containing the signature of the master, each original copy shall prevail against its signatory.

If there is a discrepancy between the charter-party and the bill of lading, the stipulations of the charter-party shall prevail in the relations of the lessor with the charterer.

However, in the relations of the charterer with the shipper, the bill of lading alone shall govern, unless it expressly provides for the adoption of a charter-party.

A through bill of lading, which is that delivered by a first carrier who undertakes to forward the goods to the place of destination in successive stages, binds its issuer until the end of the voyage to all the obligations arising therefrom.

He is bound, in particular, to warrant the acts of the successive carriers who take delivery of the goods. Each of the latter shall be liable only for the loss, damage, and delay occurring during his own voyage.

If the nature of the goods or the conditions of their carriage require the conclusion of special agreements, all the agreed stipulations relating to the rights and obligations of the carrier shall be given effect so long as they are not contrary to public policy, provided that no negotiable bill of lading is issued and that the agreement is inserted in an instrument containing the phrase "non-negotiable".

Handwritten stipulations shall prevail over printed stipulations in general. Where both a charter-party and a bill of lading are drawn up together, and a dispute subsequently arises between handwritten stipulations and printed stipulations, the bill of lading shall prevail over the charter-party.

The provisions of this Title shall apply only to maritime carriage entailing the delivery of bills of lading and from the time the goods are loaded on board the vessel until their discharge at the place of destination. Nor shall they apply to charter-parties.

However, if the vessel is chartered under a charter-party, they shall apply to such bills of lading as may be issued, and these provisions cannot be applied to goods loaded on the deck of the vessel pursuant to the contract of carriage, nor to live animals.

The carrier is bound before the commencement of the voyage.

1) To put the vessel in good order so as to be seaworthy.

2) To equip and supply it with appropriate tackle, men, and provisions.

3) To clean and put in good condition the holds (cargo holds), the cold and refrigerated chambers, and all other parts of the vessel intended for the loading of goods.

The carrier warrants against all loss, deterioration, and damage befalling the goods unless he proves that such loss, deterioration, and damage result from the following:

1) From faults in navigation attributable to the master, seamen, pilots, or other servants.

2) From latent defects in the vessel.

3) From a strike or the corresponding lockout, or anything that obstructs work wholly or partially, and from any cause whatsoever of stoppage or hindrance.

4) From acts constituting a fortuitous event or force majeure.

5) From an inherent vice in the goods or a defect in their packing or marking (branding), or from wastage during the voyage to the extent of the volume and weight allowed by custom at the ports of destination.

6) From rendering maritime assistance or salvage, or an attempt aimed thereat, or if the vessel happens to deviate while performing this act.

However, in all the excepted cases above, the shipper may prove that the losses or damages result from the fault of the carrier or his servants if the latter do not benefit from the first subparagraph of this article.

The liability of the carrier resulting from losses and damages befalling the goods may under no circumstances exceed, per package or unit, an amount to be fixed by a decree issued in the week following the publication of this Law, unless the shipper declares the nature of these goods and their value prior to their loading onto the vessel.

This declaration shall be inserted in the bill of lading and shall be binding upon the carrier unless the latter proves the contrary. If the carrier contests the accuracy of the declaration at the time it is made, he may insert reasoned reservations in the bill of lading.

The effect of these reservations is to place the proof of the true value upon the sender or the receiver. Any stipulation whereby the carrier limits his liability to an amount lower than that prescribed by this article shall be deemed null and void. The amount prescribed above may be revised by a decree taken on the basis of international currency fluctuations.

Every stipulation inserted in a bill of lading or in any document of carriage by sea created in Lebanon shall be deemed null and of no effect where its direct or indirect object is to exonerate the carrier from the liability imposed upon him by the general law or by this Law, or to shift the burden of proof from the person upon whom it is placed by the laws in force or by this Law, or to contravene the rules of jurisdiction.

Every stipulation leaving to the carrier the benefit of insurance on the goods, or any other stipulation of the same nature, shall be deemed a stipulation of exoneration.
If the shipper knowingly makes a false declaration as to the value of the goods, the carrier shall incur no liability for loss or damage sustained by such goods.

If goods of an inflammable, explosive or dangerous nature are shipped on board the vessel, to the shipment of which the carrier or his agent would not have consented had they known of their nature, the carrier may, at any time and place, and after drawing up a reasoned report, land them from the vessel, destroy them or render them innocuous without his act giving rise to compensation.

Moreover, the shipper shall be liable for the damage and expenses which may result from the loading of such goods. If, however, the carrier knew of the nature of such goods when he consented to their being loaded on board the vessel, he shall not be entitled to land them therefrom, nor to destroy them or render them innocuous unless they become a cause of endangering the vessel or her cargo.

No compensation shall be due save for general average, if it occurs.

If the goods are lost or damaged, the receiver thereof must address written reservations to the carrier or his agent at the port of discharge and at the time of delivery at the latest.

Failing which, he shall be presumed to have received the goods as described in the bill of lading.

If, however, the loss or damage is not apparent, notification of such reservations shall be valid if made within a time limit of three days after delivery. Holidays shall not be included in the computation of this time limit.

The carrier shall always be entitled to demand a contradictory survey of the goods upon their receipt.

Whatever the case may be, the right to bring an action against the carrier on account of loss or damage shall be barred by prescription one year after the delivery of the goods, and if delivery has not taken place, one year from the day on which they ought to have been delivered.

After the expiry of one year from the end of the voyage, the right to any action vacating from a charterparty or a contract of carriage shall be barred by prescription, subject to the provisions of the preceding Article.

The following shall be barred by prescription:

One year after the end of the voyage, the right to any pecuniary action relating to freight.

One year after delivery, the right to any pecuniary action arising from the supply of food to seamen by order of the master or from the supply of things necessary for fitting out and victualling.

One year after the receipt of the works, the right to any pecuniary action relating to the wages of workmen and the execution of works.

One year after the arrival of the vessel, the right to any action arising from the delivery of goods.

The expenses of the passengers' food shall be included in the passage money unless there is an agreement to the contrary, in which latter case the master shall be bound to supply the necessary provisions for a fair price.
If the passage ticket or the contract is drawn up in the name of the passenger, the latter may not transfer his right to another person without the consent of the master.

The carriage of the passenger's luggage shall be subject to the provisions governing the carriage of goods unless the passenger retains custody thereof. In the latter case, the master shall not be deemed liable for loss and damage unless caused by the act of the crew.
The passage money shall be due even if the passenger does not undertake the voyage or undertakes only part thereof, unless force majeure prevents the performance of the carriage.

If departure does not take place on the appointed day owing to the act of the master, the passenger shall be entitled to compensation for the damage sustained by him, and the rescission of the contract may be ordered.

If the voyage becomes impossible owing to a prohibition of trade with the port of destination, or owing to blockade or any case of force majeure, the contract of passage shall be made room for and there shall be no rescinded room for one party to compensate the other.

If force majeure prevents the vessel from reaching the port of destination, the master shall only be entitled to recover the expenses of food, and he shall not be entitled to the passage money unless he arranges for the passenger to reach the place of destination.

If the interruption of the voyage results from the fault of the master, the latter shall bear the expenses of food and shall be bound to arrange for the carriage of the passenger to the place of destination.

If the master is compelled to have the vessel repaired during the voyage, the passenger shall be bound to await the completion of the repairs or to pay the passage money in full, and he shall be entitled throughout the duration of the works to free lodging and food unless the master offers him the completion of his voyage on board another vessel of the same class.
If an accident befalls the passenger during the voyage, the carrier shall be liable for such accident unless he proves that it resulted from force majeure or from the fault of the passenger.
If the passenger dies during the voyage, the master shall be bound to take the necessary measures with a view to preserving the luggage on board the vessel and delivering it to the heirs.
The passenger, while on board the vessel, shall be bound to comply with the regulations established by the master and to obey the orders of the vessel.

After the expiry of a time limit of one year by prescription the right to any action arising out of the contract of carriage of passengers.

Actions arising from the contract of carriage of the passenger's luggage shall be subject to the provisions of Article 215 of this Law.

If a vessel is towed and makes use of her own propelling power, her master shall be liable towards any third party for the fault of the master of the tug unless he proves that the latter was not under his direction.

However, this liability on his part leaves intact his right of recourse against the master of the tug if it is proved that this master committed a personal fault.

If a collision occurs between sea-going vessels or between sea-going vessels and inland navigation vessels, the compensation for damage caused to the vessels and to the things and persons on board shall be paid in accordance with the following provisions, regardless of the waters in which the collision occurred.

If the collision is fortuitous, or if it is caused by force majeure, or if there is doubt as to its causes, the damage shall be borne by the party who has suffered it, and this provision shall continue to apply if the vessels, or one of them, were at anchor at the time of the collision.
If the collision is caused by the fault of one of the vessels, compensation for the damages shall be borne by the party liable for such collision.

If the fault is common, the liability of each vessel shall be in proportion to the gravity of the fault committed by her. However, if the circumstances prevent the establishment of this proportion, or if the faults appear to be equivalent, the liability shall be apportioned in equal shares. The damage caused to the vessels, or to their cargoes, or to the luggage or other property of the crew, passengers or any other person on board the vessel, shall be borne by the vessels in fault in the aforesaid proportion and without joint and several liability towards third parties. The vessels in fault shall be jointly and severally liable towards third parties for damage arising from death or injury, saving the right of recourse for the vessel which pays a share exceeding the share finally incumbent upon her under the first paragraph of this Article.
Where a collision occurs and is caused by the fault of a pilot, liability shall remain as established in the preceding Articles even if the presence of such pilot is compulsory.

The preceding provisions shall apply, where no collision has occurred, to compensation for damage which a vessel causes to another vessel or to things or persons on board thereof by carrying out a manoeuvre, by omitting a manoeuvre, or by failing to observe the regulations.

The master of every vessel which has collided with another shall render assistance to the other vessel, her crew, and her passengers in so far as he is able to do so without exposing his vessel, his crew, and his passengers to serious danger.

The master shall also inform the other vessel, so far as possible, of the name of his vessel, her port of registry, the port from which she comes, and the port to which she is bound. The owner of the vessel shall not be held liable by reason solely of a breach of the preceding provisions.
The provisions of this Title shall not apply to warships and State vessels appropriated exclusively to a public service.

An action for compensation for damage resulting from a collision shall not be subject to a protest or to any other formality. No special presumption of fault shall arise in respect of liability for the collision.

Where a collision occurs, the plaintiff shall have the option to bring the action before the court of the defendant or before the court of the port of registry of the colliding vessel. The court having jurisdiction over the first Lebanese port entered by either of the two vessels after their collision shall be competent to carry out any inquiry or technical survey. In Lebanese territorial waters, jurisdiction shall vest in the court of the place of the collision.

All actions for compensation for damage resulting from a collision shall be barred by prescription upon the expiry of a period of two years after the casualty.

However, the right of action provided for in the third paragraph of Article 236 shall be barred by prescription after the expiry of one year from the day of payment.

Every act of assistance or salvage performed by a vessel by way of service to another vessel which is in danger, to the things on board such vessel, and to her freight and the passage money of her passengers, even where her crew has abandoned her, shall be subject to the following provisions.

Every act of assistance or salvage which has had a useful result shall give rise to a right to equitable remuneration. No remuneration shall be due if the rendering of assistance has had no beneficial result. In no case shall the sum to be paid exceed the value of the property salved.
Persons who take part in assistance operations shall have no right to any remuneration if the vessel assisted has expressly and reasonably forbidden them to assist her.

A tug shall have no right to any remuneration for assistance to or salvage of the vessel towed by her or her cargo unless she has rendered exceptional services which cannot be considered as the performance of the contract of towage.
Remuneration shall be due notwithstanding that the assistance or salvage has taken place between vessels belonging to the same owner.

The amount of the remuneration shall be fixed by agreement between the parties and, failing agreement, by the court. The same shall apply to the proportion in which such remuneration is to be apportioned amongst the salvors or amongst the owners, master, and crew of each salving vessel.

Where the salving vessel is a foreign vessel, the apportionment amongst her owner, her master, and persons in her service shall be regulated by the law of her State.

Every agreement as to assistance or salvage entered into at the moment and under the influence of danger may, at the request of either of the contracting parties, be annulled or modified by the court if it considers that the conditions agreed upon are not equitable.

In all cases, where it is proved that the consent of one of the parties was vitiated by fraud or concealment, or where the remuneration is, in either direction, excessive and out of proportion to the service rendered, the agreement may be annulled or modified by the court at the request of the party concerned.

The court shall fix the remuneration according to the circumstances of the case, on the basis of:

(a) First:

The measure of success obtained, the efforts and deserts of the salvors, the danger run by the assisted vessel, by her passengers, her crew, and her cargo, by the salvors, and by the salving vessel, the time expended, the expenses and damage incurred, the risks of liability and other risks run by the salvors, and the value of the property exposed to them, due regard being had, the case arising, to the special appropriation of the assisting vessel for that purpose.

(b) Secondly, the value of the property lost.

The same provisions shall apply to the apportionment provided for in the second paragraph of Article 251.

The court may reduce or disallow the remuneration if it appears that the salvors have by their fault rendered the salvage or assistance necessary or have been guilty of theft, receiving stolen goods, or other acts of fraud.

No remuneration shall be due in respect of persons saved. Salvors of human life who have intervened on the occasion of the same dangers shall be entitled to a fair share of the remuneration awarded to the salvors of the vessel, the cargo, and their accessories.

Repealed by the Law of 21 December 1954 and replaced by the following provisions):

An action claiming remuneration for assistance or salvage shall be barred by prescription after the expiry of two years from the day on which the operations of assistance or salvage are terminated.

This period shall not run if the assisted or lost vessel has not been arrested in Lebanese waters.

Every master who observes a person at sea in danger of drowning and refrains from assisting him, when he can do so without exposing his vessel, her crew, and her passengers to serious danger, shall be punished by imprisonment from one month to two years and by a fine from one hundred pounds to three thousand pounds, or by one of these two penalties.

Averages are all damage or loss occurring during the maritime voyage to the vessel or the cargo.

As well as all extraordinary or unusual expenses which may be incurred to ensure the safety of the voyage.
In the absence of special agreement between all the parties concerned, averages shall be adjusted in accordance with the following provisions:
Averages are of two kinds: particular averages and general averages.
Particular averages are all averages which do not fulfil the conditions required in the following Articles. Such averages shall be borne by the owner of the thing which has suffered the damage.

General averages are damage, loss of things, and extraordinary expenses resulting from a sacrifice intentionally made by the master for the common benefit and to meet a peril to which the voyage was exposed. It shall not be required that a useful result be obtained therefrom, save in the cases provided for in Article 263.

Such is the case with:

1- Damages-averages, which are averages caused:

(a) To the cargo by reason of the jettison of goods into the sea, their use as fuel to enable the completion of the voyage, their discharge onto a lighter to lighten or refloat the vessel, and the carrying out of nautical operations to extinguish a fire.

(b) And to the vessel by reason of the loss of apparel and accessories, the intentional stranding of the vessel ashore for the purpose of saving the cargo, the disabling and damaging of the vessel for the purpose of saving the cargo, and the forcing of sails or of steam when the vessel is stranded ashore.

2- And expenses-averages, which are extraordinary expenses paid by the master for the safety of the voyage, such as expenses of refloating, assisting, and towing a damaged vessel, expenses of putting into a port of refuge necessitated by a maritime peril, expenses of maintenance and wages of the crew paid by reason of an extraordinary event, expenses paid in substitution for an expense which would have been allowable as general average provided that they do not exceed the amount of the expense replaced, and finally the expenses of adjusting the general average.
Only such damage, losses, and expenses as are the direct consequence of an act having the character of general average shall be admitted as general average.
The burden of proving that an expense or loss ought to be admitted as general average shall lie upon the party claiming such admission.

No regard shall be had to a special agreement unless it is approved by everyone having an interest in the voyage, and in contrary cases maritime averages shall be settled in accordance with the rules of apportionment set forth below, subject to the application of special agreements between the interested parties.

In order to give rise to apportionment, the whole or part of the vessel and the cargo must have been saved, unless one of them has been totally sacrificed for the preservation of the safety of the other.

If the common peril is the result either of an inherent defect in the vessel or in the goods, or of the fault of the master or the shippers, the damages and expenses which have the character of general average shall likewise give rise to apportionment for the remaining interested parties. And those parties shall retain their right of recourse, for the amount which they pay for their share, against those who bear the liability for the inherent defect and the fault.

Those persons may not in any case whatsoever claim to have their own particular damages and expenses included among the general average. However, the ship operator who is exonerated from liability for the faults of the master in navigation by a clause inserted in the charter-party or in the bill of lading may submit a claim for apportionment, provided that the fault of the master in navigation was the source of the common peril.

Goods for which no bill of lading has been drawn up or for which the master has not given an acknowledgment of receipt (a receipt notice) shall not be counted as general average if they are sacrificed, but they shall contribute if they are saved.

The same rule shall apply to goods in respect of which a false declaration has been made, unless the interested party proves his good faith. Goods sacrificed or damaged which have been declared at less than their true value shall be counted as averages on the basis of the declared value, but they shall contribute on the basis of their true value.

Goods stowed on the deck of the vessel contrary to maritime usages shall contribute if they are saved.

If, however, they are sacrificed, their owner shall not be permitted to submit a claim for apportionment unless he proves that he did not consent to this method of stowage.

This provision shall not apply to short coastal navigation.

Postal dispatches of every kind, the luggage and personal effects of the seamen and passengers, the wages of the seamen, the provisions of the vessel, and in general all things which may properly be carried without a bill of lading shall be exempted from contribution. If, however, they are sacrificed, their value shall be reimbursed by way of apportionment.
Every interested party may discharge himself from the obligation of contribution by abandoning the property subject to apportionment prior to any taking of delivery.

The adjustment of maritime averages shall take place at the last port of destination of the cargo which is on board the vessel at the time of the sacrifice or at the place where the voyage is broken up, and in accordance with the law of that port.

It shall cover the values existing at the time of discharge and having regard to the condition of the saved objects. It shall consist of three parts.

1) Determination of the creditor mass.

2) Determination of the debtor mass.

3) Finding the proportion in which the amount of the first mass is distributed over the second mass.
The adjustment shall be carried out by experts appointed by the judge of urgent matters if all the interested parties do not agree upon them.
If the adjustment is not accepted by all the interested parties, it shall be submitted for homologation by the court upon the request of the most diligent party.

There shall be included in the creditor mass the expenses of the master, the amount of the damage sustained by the vessel, the price of the sacrificed goods, the lost freight, and the expenses of the adjustment of the maritime averages.

The amount counted as general average by reason of loss or damage sustained by the vessel shall consist of the cost of repair or replacement, subject to the deduction therefrom of the difference between new and old as is customary.

Temporary repairs, however, shall not be subject to deduction. If there is no repair or replacement involved, the amount counted as average shall be determined by appraisal.

Sacrificed goods or the damages sustained by them shall be appraised according to the current price at the place of loading, provided that their owner pays the freight after deduction of the expenses of discharge and customs duties, where applicable.
If the loss of the freight of the vessel is counted as general average, the expenses of collecting it and any substitute for such freight must be deducted from its gross amount at risk.

There shall be included in the debtor mass:

- The goods at their full value if they are saved, or at the full value estimated for them at the port of destination if they are sacrificed, after deduction of the expenses, including customs duties and the freight of the vessel, unless it is stipulated that the freight is earned whatever casualties may occur.

- The vessel at its net true value at the port where it comes to rest, after deduction of the expenses.

- The freight of the vessel and the passage money of the passengers at risk at two-thirds of their gross amount, except for the freight of the vessel if it is stipulated that it is earned whatever casualties may occur.
The master may refuse to deliver the goods unless sufficient security is provided to him for the payment of the contribution.

The contributions due to the ship operator shall have a lien on the goods or the proceeds realized therefrom for a period of fifteen days after their delivery, if they have not passed into the hands of a third party.

The owners of the sacrificed goods shall have a lien on the vessel for the amount of the contributions incumbent upon it for its operator and on its freight at risk.

Distribution shall take place pro rata in proportion to the claim due. In the event of the insolvency of one of the contributors, his share must be distributed among the others in proportion to the claims of each of them.

All actions for general average contribution for loss or damage in respect of which a reasoned protest has not been made within a period of three days, excluding holidays, beginning from the delivery of the goods, shall be dismissed.

The right to an action for apportionment shall lapse by prescription after two years from the arrival of the vessel at the last port of destination of the goods which were on board the vessel at the time of the sacrifice or at the place where the voyage was broken up.

A contract of bottomry or respondentia is a contract whereby a sum is lent on the security of the vessel or the cargo on condition that the loan shall be lost to the lender if the objects assigned to the debt perish by a marine casualty of force majeure, and that the loan shall be repaid to him with the maritime interest, that is, the agreed interest even if its rate exceeds the legal limit, if those objects arrive safely.
A bottomry or respondentia loan may only be contracted with the master during the voyage in order to meet the expenses of repair or to satisfy the other needs of the vessel or the cargo

The necessity of incurring expenses useful to the vessel or to the cargo must be verified in Lebanon by the justice of the peace, and abroad by the consular authority if one exists, and failing that, by the local magistrate. The competent judge shall supervise the effecting of the loan by public tender, and it shall be awarded to the lender who offers the lowest rate of maritime interest.

Authorization may, however, be granted to contract the loan by private agreement where the circumstances so require.

A contract of bottomry or respondentia may be effected upon the vessel, upon the cargo, and upon its freight jointly or separately. If the expenses are for the benefit of the cargo, the master may pledge the goods.

And if they are for the benefit of the vessel, the master may not borrow on the security of the cargo except after exhausting the credit which the vessel affords him.

If the master observes the rules laid down in the preceding articles, he shall not be personally liable for the loan. The owner of the vessel upon which the loan is effected shall be liable for the loan, while retaining his right of abandonment and limitation of liability provided for in Article 94.

And the owner of the goods upon which the loan is effected shall be liable for the loan, while retaining the right to abandon the goods to the lender.

The instrument evidencing the loan must state the date, the sum borrowed, the stipulated interest, the property upon which the loan is secured, the names of each of the contracting parties, of the vessel, and of the master, and the term of the loan.

The contract shall be made out to a specified person, or to order, or to bearer; and if the word "to order" is inserted in the contract, the guarantee of the endorsers shall not include the interest unless there is an agreement to the contrary.
The lender may recover the loan if the property upon which the loan is secured perishes due to an inherent defect or due to the act of the borrower or his servants.

The lender shall not contribute to particular average affecting the property upon which the loan is secured, yet in the event of shipwreck he shall bear a share of the expenses of salving the property upon which the loan is secured in proportion to the amount of the debt.

If general average occurs, the amount of the loan shall not be added to the contributing values, and the adjustment of contribution among the vessel, her freight, and the cargo shall be carried out as if there were no bottomry contract in the matter; however, the lender shall contribute to the relief of the owners of the property upon which the loan is secured in proportion to the amount of the debt.
If several loans are contracted on the security of the same property, a later loan shall have priority over an earlier one.
Every right of action arising out of a bottomry contract shall be barred by prescription after two years beginning from the date on which the debt falls due.

Marine insurance is a contract whereby the insurer agrees to indemnify the insured against damage sustained by him in the course of a sea voyage resulting from an actual loss of some value in consideration of the payment of a premium, provided that such indemnity shall not exceed the value of the property lost.

All provisions of this Title which are not expressly declared to be applicable notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary, or for which non-observance is not declared to entail nullity, shall serve solely as an interpretation of the intention of the contracting parties and may be derogated from by an express stipulation.

The contract of insurance shall be drawn up in writing and in two original copies. There must be stated therein the following:

- The date of the contract of insurance, and whether it was concluded before or after noon.

- The name of the applicant for insurance, on his own behalf or on behalf of another, and the name of his place of residence.

- The risks which the insurer assumes and the limits of their duration.

- The sum insured.

- The amount of the premium or consideration for the insurance.

It shall be signed by the insurer and the insured, or by the insurance broker on behalf of the insured. It may be made out to a named person, or to order, or to bearer. Each of the contracting parties shall be entitled to receive a certified true copy of the insurance policy.

Insurers may only be summoned before the court of the place where the contract was signed. However, if the contract was signed by an agent, the insured may bring an action before the court of the domicile of the insurer.

If more than half of the insured value was underwritten in one place, the insured may summon all the other insurers before the court of that place which has already been seized of an action, for the purpose of having the same action adjudicated against them.

Any concealment of information or false declaration on the part of the insured at the time of entering into the contract, and any discrepancy between the contract of insurance and the shipping documents which would diminish the estimation of the risk, shall annul the insurance even in the absence of fraudulent intent.

The insurance shall be annulled even where the concealment of information, discrepancy, or false declaration has no effect on the damage or on the loss of the subject-matter insured. The insurer shall retain the entire premium if the insured had fraudulent intent, and half of it in the absence of such intent.
The insured must notify the insurer, under pain of the same penalty, of events subsequent to the contract which may modify the estimation of the risk on the part of the insurer.

The insurer is entitled to set up against the holder of the insurance policy, even if it is made out to order or to bearer, the defences appertaining thereto which he could have invoked against the original insured had the transfer not taken place.

The contract of insurance may always be rescinded at the will of the insured so long as the risks have not begun to run.

An insured who cannot prove a case of force majeure shall pay to the insurer, by way of a lump-sum indemnity, half of the premium stipulated in the contract.

If the subject-matter of the insurance is goods for an outward and homeward voyage, and after the vessel reaches her first destination no homeward cargo is shipped, or the shipment of the homeward cargo is not completed, the insurer shall receive two-thirds of the agreed premium and no more, unless there is an agreement to the contrary.

In the event of the bankruptcy of the insured or his notorious cessation of payments, or in the event of his failure to pay a premium that has fallen due, the insurers shall be entitled, after an unavailing formal notice served at the place of residence of the insured requiring payment or the provision of acceptable security within a period of twenty-four hours, to rescind by simple notice, even by registered letter, effective from the latest communication, every current insurance specified in the notice, provided that the insurers waive the premium in proportion to the remaining duration of the risks, while the excess remains a debt due to them.

However, the formal notice and the notice of rescission may be effected together in a single instrument. The insured shall have the same rights in the event of the bankruptcy of the insurer or his notorious cessation of payments. The provisions of the first paragraph shall not apply to a third party in good faith who duly holds the bill of lading and the insurance policy or its addendum.

The public sale of the vessel shall ipso jure suspend the insurance on the day of the sale, and the insurance shall continue in the event of a private sale affecting less than half of the insured value. If a private sale affects at least half of the insured value, the insurance shall not continue except with the consent of the insurers.
The chartering of the vessel shall not result in the rescission of the insurance unless there is an agreement to the contrary.

The insured must notify the insurers of the news of a casualty or loss within a period of three days from his receipt of the news.

He must mitigate as far as possible the effect of the risk, take all conservatory measures, supervise the operations of salving the insured property or carry out such operations, and preserve every right of action against third parties who are liable.

An insured who engages in salvage shall retain his rights to indemnity and abandonment. He shall be entitled to the reimbursement of his expenses upon his mere affirmation, subject to fraud proved by the insurer.

The insurer in turn may himself take all conservatory or salvage measures without anyone having the right to invoke against him that he has performed an act of ownership.

Receivers must apply to the agents or representatives of the insurers named in the policy, if any, and failing them to the competent local authority, in order to survey the losses and marine damages, under pain of inadmissibility of the action.

They must also, under pain of the same penalty, complete the conduct of these surveys within a period of eight days following the day on which the carrier places the goods at their disposal or at the disposal of their representatives or agents, provided that this period shall not exceed thirty days beginning from the date of arrival of the goods at the destination.

However, this period of thirty days shall not run against a receiver who proves that he was unaware of the arrival of the goods at the destination.

If contracts of insurance on goods are evidenced by floating policies, that is, open cover policies, the insured is bound to declare during the currency of the policy all shipments loaded on his own behalf or on behalf of other persons who have entrusted him with insuring their goods, insofar as the insurance covers them. If the insured fails to fulfil this obligation, the contract may be cancelled upon the request of the insurer, who shall retain the premiums paid in all cases and shall be entitled to payment of the premiums relating to the undeclared shipments.

If the declaration relates to goods insured on behalf of a third party, it shall have no effect if made after the occurrence of a supervening casualty.

A contract of insurance may be concluded for the benefit of an unspecified person. This clause shall operate both as a contract of insurance for the benefit of the person who signs the policy and as a stipulation for another for the benefit of the beneficiary, whether known or future. The signatory of the policy relating to insurance concluded for the benefit of an unspecified person shall alone be liable towards the insurer for the payment of the premium; however, the defences which the insurer may set up against the signatory may also be invoked against the person who benefits from the insurance.

Every interested person may contract insurance on a vessel and its appurtenances, a vessel under construction and the parts prepared for that vessel and located at the factory, the costs of fitting out, provisions, seamen's wages, freight, sums contracted under a bottomry loan, goods, money and securities laden on the vessel, expected profit, and in general all things estimable in money and exposed to the perils of navigation.

The agreed value of the vessel includes undividedly all its accessories, in particular provisions, advances to seamen, tackle and all disbursements, unless it can be proved that certain of those disbursements relate to an interest distinct from the interest of ownership of the vessel.
Where the subject-matter of the insurance is the net freight, the amount of such freight shall be assessed at sixty per cent of the gross freight if the contract does not stipulate a fixed sum.

Expected profit shall be fixed at one tenth of the value at the place of departure, unless the insurers expressly agree to a higher valuation, in which case the proportion of that allowance must be specified in the policy.

Where the value of the goods is not fixed in the contract, it may be proved by means of invoices and books; failing which, the goods shall be valued according to the current price at the time and place of loading, together with all duties and expenses paid up to the time they are carried onto the vessel, freight earned whatever the contingency, the insurance premium, and expected profit where applicable.

The same applies to the valuation of the hull of the vessel, its keel, rigging and gear, which shall be determined on the basis of their value on the day the risks commence. Tackle, provisions and all things estimable in money shall be valued according to their value at the place and time the risks commence.
The insurer may always prove that the agreed value exceeds the true value of the insured subject-matter, even where he has accepted the insured's valuation in the policy.

The insurer may reinsure with another person the risks which he has insured. Such reinsurance shall be subject to the provisions of this Title, and the insurer shall remain solely liable towards the insured.
The insured may insure the insurance premium.

Any contract of insurance effected after the loss or arrival of the insured objects shall be void if it is proved that news of the loss or news of the arrival had reached either the place where the insured was before he gave the order for insurance, or the place where the contract was signed before the insurer signed it. Where the insurance is effected on "lost or not lost" terms, which clause is permissible only in the insurance of an equipped vessel, the contract shall not be annulled unless proof is adduced that the insured knew of the loss of the vessel or that the insurer knew of its arrival before the signing of the contract.

If proof is established against the insured, the latter shall pay the insurer double the premium. If it is established against the insurer, the latter shall pay the insured a sum equal to double the agreed premium.

Insurance effected by an agent shall be void if that agent could have known of the news. It shall likewise be void if the principal knew of it. Where the principal learned of the news after giving the order, he must forthwith send a countermand, by telegram where necessary.

The insurance shall be valid if signed before the arrival of the countermand.

Where the master is permitted to load goods for his own account on the vessel which he commands, he must, if he insures such goods, prove to the insurers by all means the purchase of the goods and produce a bill of lading therefor signed by two senior members of the crew.

Where there is no bill of lading, or where the bill of lading contains clauses limiting the probative value of the document issued by the master, the insured must produce other instruments proving the shipment, such as purchase invoices, manifests, copies delivered by the customs authorities, consignment notes and letters. Oral evidence shall be admissible in the absence of all other evidence.

Marine insurance must be a contract of indemnity notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary. It may not place the insured person, after the occurrence of the casualties, in a better financial position than that in which he would have been had the casualty not occurred.

A person is entitled to effect as many contracts of insurance as he wishes on the same object, provided that he derives from the accumulation of such contracts no benefit exceeding the loss which he has sustained.

Where insurance is contracted for a sum of money exceeding the value of the insured object and there is fraud or deceit on the part of the insured, the contract may be annulled upon the application of the insurer, who shall be entitled to the whole premium by way of damages.

Where there is neither fraud nor deceit, the contract shall be deemed valid up to the value of the insured objects as valued or as agreed upon. The insurer shall not be entitled to receive the premium for the excess amount, but he may obtain damages where applicable.

Where the total of the sums insured under several contracts exceeds the value of the insured objects, the contracts may be annulled in accordance with the preceding Article if there is fraud or deceit on the part of the insured.

Where, however, there is neither fraud nor deceit, all the contracts shall be valid and each of them shall produce its effects in proportion to the sum contracted for, up to the full value of the insured object.

This provision may be set aside by a clause in the policy adopting the rule of order of dates or stipulating the joint and several liability of the insurers.

Where the contract of insurance covers only a part of the value of the insured object, the insured person shall be deemed to remain his own insurer for the remaining part, and shall consequently bear a proportionate part of the damage, unless it is expressly stipulated that the insured person is entitled - within the limits of the sum insured - to receive full indemnity if the damage does not exceed the insured value.

Insurance shall be deemed to be of a marine nature merely by being contracted on a craft designated as a "vessel", even though such craft does not engage in maritime navigation. The insurance shall cover the vessel during its repair and its stay in basins and dry docks and in general at any place whatsoever within the limits of navigation specified in the policy.

Insurance of goods shall retain the character of marine insurance even if they are subjected to carriage by land or river, provided that such carriage is only accessory in relation to the carriage by sea.

The insurers shall bear the risks of all loss and damage caused to the insured objects by storm, shipwreck, stranding, collision, forced putting into port, forced change of route, of voyage and of vessel, jettison, fire, explosion, pillage, damage wilfully caused by the crew, theft, and in general all marine casualties and accidents. The risks of civil or foreign war shall not be borne by the insurer.

Where there is an agreement to the contrary, the insurer shall be liable for all damages and losses caused to the insured objects by hostilities, reprisals, arrest, capture and molestation by any government whatsoever, whether friendly or enemy, recognized or unrecognized, and in general by all casualties and acts of war of a coercive nature. It shall be incumbent upon the insurers of ordinary risks to prove the war risk.

The insurer shall be liable for the expenses of refloating, the expenses of assisting a vessel exposed to an imminent peril, the expenses of salvage at sea, and the expenses of towage when the vessel is taken to a port for the purpose of being repaired.

The provisions of this Article shall not apply to stranding resulting from the normal action of the tide, nor to casual stranding either in maritime canals or in rivers and streams above the places reached by the tide.

Where the expenses of temporary putting into port constitute particular average, the provisions and wages of the crew shall not be borne by the insurer. However, if the vessel is taken to a better port than the port of temporary refuge for the purpose of undergoing repairs there at the expense of the insurers, the provisions and wages of the crew and the expenses of towage shall be borne by the insurers.

The same applies to the vessel if it stays in a port of temporary refuge awaiting spare parts necessary for the completion of the voyage and when the repairs are borne by the insurers.

Where the vessel collides with another vessel belonging to the insured or receives salvage assistance therefrom, the settlement shall take place as if the vessels belonged to different shipowners. Questions of liability for collision or remuneration for services rendered shall be determined as against the parties interested in the hull of the vessel by a sole arbitrator appointed by agreement of the insured parties, if any, and failing that, by decision of the President of the Court sitting as a judge of urgent matters.

The same shall apply to the collision of the vessel with a fixed or floating body belonging to the insured.
Contribution to general average shall be borne by the insurers in proportion to the value which they insure after deducting the amount of particular average payable by them, where applicable.

Insurers shall be discharged from all claims for delay in dispatch or arrival of the goods, for differences in prices, and for obstacles arising in respect of the commercial transaction of the insured for any cause whatsoever.

The insurer shall not be liable for loss and damage resulting from intentional or inexcusable faults committed by the insured or his representatives. Any agreement to the contrary shall be deemed null and void. The insurer of the hull of the vessel shall not be liable for the consequences of the fraud and deceit of the master where the latter has been chosen by the shipowner.

By way of exception to what has been stated regarding the insurance of damage intentionally caused by the seamen, and contrary thereto, the insurers shall be discharged:

1) From acts of fraud and deceit committed by the master and from all casualties of every kind resulting from breach of blockade, smuggling, and prohibited or clandestine trade, unless the master has been changed without the consent of the shipowner or his representative and replaced by another person other than the chief mate.

2) And from all consequences entailed upon the vessel by any act whatsoever performed by the master or the seamen ashore.

Damage and loss resulting from an inherent vice in the insured property shall not be borne by the insurer unless the contrary is stipulated, save where the insurance is upon the hull of the vessel and there was a latent defect in the vessel which a diligent shipowner was neither able to foresee nor to prevent.

Nevertheless, such damage and such loss shall be borne by the insurer if the voyage is subjected to an extraordinary delay by reason of a peril insured against by the insurer, provided that the damage is caused by the delay itself.
The insurer shall not be liable for damage caused by the insured property to other property or persons unless the contrary is stipulated.

The risks of third-party actions brought against the vessel by reason of its collision with another vessel or its striking against a floating craft, dykes, quays, stockades, or other fixed bodies shall place upon the insurers nine-tenths of the damages awarded, up to a maximum of nine-tenths of the sum insured. The insured shall bear one-tenth of the damages, and he is prohibited from insuring this one-tenth. Should a breach of this prohibition occur, he shall suffer the deduction of a second one-tenth.

Insurers shall be discharged from any action brought against them by any person whomsoever and for any cause whatsoever on the ground of damage or prejudice relating to the cargo of the insured vessel and its engagements, as well as from all actions brought on the ground of death or injury and on the ground of any casualty or bodily harm.

Where the vessel is lost and the master is the owner or one of the owners thereof, payment of his share of the insurance shall be deferred until the production of the certificate establishing the result of the administrative inquiry which must be conducted concerning his conduct.

If it is established by such inquiry that the loss is attributable to the faults of the master, even though he is not convicted of fraud or deceit, the insurers may be discharged from the insured share of the master after paying him by way of settlement fifty per cent of the indemnity.

Where the insurance is upon the hull of the vessel and the duration of the risks is not specified in the contract, the risks under an insurance concluded for the voyage shall run from the moment the vessel sails or weighs anchor and shall cease at the moment it casts anchor or is moored at the place of destination; provided, however, that if it loads goods, the risks shall run from the moment loading of the goods commences and shall cease as soon as discharge is completed, without exceeding a period of fifteen days after arrival at the place of destination, unless goods are shipped at that place for another voyage before the expiry of such period, in which case the risks shall cease forthwith.

Quarantine shall be deemed to be part of the voyage which necessitates it. However, if the vessel insured for the voyage proceeds to perform quarantine at a place other than the place of destination, the insurer shall be entitled to an increase in premium of three-quarters per cent per month from the day of departure for the quarantine station until the day of return.

The same increases in premium shall apply in the event of a vessel staying off the port of destination if it finds it blockaded, or in the event of its departing therefrom for another port.

In such case, the insurers shall continue to bear the risks during the entire duration of the stay and departure, provided that such extension does not exceed six months starting from the date of arrival off the blockaded port; however, they shall not be liable for any expense or increase in expenditure resulting from such departure and such stay. The insured shall always be entitled, if he so wishes, to put an end to the risks before the six months.

In the case of insurance at a linked premium, which is an insurance concluded against risks occurring on the outward and return voyages, a stay of four months without increase in premium shall be granted starting from the moment the vessel calls at the first port from which it is bound to operate.

If the stay lasts more than four months, an increase of two-thirds per cent for each additional month shall be due to the insurers.

Where the insurance is upon the vessel fitted out and the duration of the risks is not specified in the contract, the risks shall run from the moment the goods leave the land for the purpose of being shipped and shall cease at the moment they are placed ashore at the place of arrival, it being understood that all risks of carriage effected directly by lighters from the land to the vessel and from the vessel to the land shall be borne by the insurers.

Where the voyage is intentionally changed after the departure of the vessel, the insurer shall be entitled to the indemnity and shall not be liable for the risks.

Where such change takes place before the voyage, the insurance shall be null and void and the insurer shall receive half of the premium stipulated in the contract by way of lump-sum compensation.

Where the vessel deviates from her course, the risks supervening on her proper course shall be covered, provided that the insurer shall have the right to prove that such risks are the consequence of such deviation.

A change of the vessel shall entail the nullity of the contract in an insurance upon the hull of the vessel. Likewise, the insurance of a fitted-out vessel shall be null and void in the event that it is intentionally changed, unless the contrary is stipulated.

Where the insured goods are loaded on the deck of the vessel, the insurers shall not be liable for the risks unless established usages of navigation permit such loading and no agreement to the contrary has been made.

In principle, the insured is bound to bring an action for average against the insurer.

However, in the event of the occurrence of casualties known as major casualties, he may abandon the insured property to the insurer and claim indemnity for total loss.
All damage and losses which do not give rise to abandonment shall be deemed average and shall be settled between the insurer and the insured in accordance with the following rules:

Where the loss of the vessel is total in respect of particular average of the vessel, the damage shall be determined with regard to the value of the vessel. In the event of loss of disbursements, the amount of the damage shall be determined with regard to the sum expended by the insured, after deducting the share which may become due to him on account of the casualty giving rise to the disbursements, where applicable.

In the determination of average, there shall only be included the price proved by invoices to have been paid for replacements and repairs which experts acknowledge to be necessary to make the vessel seaworthy, and the insured may not claim any other indemnity on the ground of depreciation in value, demurrage, or any other cause whatsoever, whether by way of particular or general average. The insurers shall be entitled to require that the replacements and repairs be carried out by way of public or written tender.

Should the insured disregard this requirement, 25 % shall be deducted from the total amount of the replacements and repairs.

The provisions and wages of the seamen shall be borne by the insurers, and the running of the premiums of insurance contracted for a fixed term shall be suspended during the period running between the date of drawing up the book of conditions and the date of the tender, provided that this period exceeds three days.

The master must not sheath the vessel and must not repair its lower part at the port of temporary call if the experts consider that it is possible to postpone the expenditure to a more suitable time. The master must also, before carrying out repairs at the port of temporary call, consult the insurance agent, if any, and failing that, the Consul of Lebanon. If such repairs are impracticable or excessively costly, he must only carry out therein the repairs that are indispensable. The insurers may send the vessel to the best-equipped port that enables the repairs to be carried out with economy of expenditure.

The vessel shall be towed to this port where necessary.

The value of the wreck must be deducted from the amount of the indemnity. The indemnity must be subjected to the deduction of new for old, and this deduction shall be determined in the insurance policies.

The assessment of maritime averages sustained by the goods shall be carried out proportionally, in gross, and according to the amount paid, that is:

1) By comparing their value after being subjected to the average with the value they would have had at the port of destination had they arrived sound, and by applying the rate of depreciation resulting therefrom to their insured value.

2) And without deducting the expenses charged upon the goods.

3) And without deducting customs duties.

Franchises restricting the effects of the insurance may be stipulated in the policies, and these franchises may be optionally determined in the policies.

Such stipulation prevents any indemnity if the damage sustained by the insured does not exceed the stipulated amount, and it shall be deducted from the indemnity if the damage exceeds this amount.
The franchise has no relation to ordinary leakage and wastage in transit as recognised by custom.
Indemnities due from the insurers shall be paid in cash thirty days after the delivery of all supporting documents.

A judgment authorising the insurer to adduce evidence of facts contrary to the facts recorded in the supporting documents shall not preclude a judgment against him for the provisional payment of the indemnities due from him, provided that the insured furnishes a surety.

The undertaking of the surety shall lapse after the expiry of two years in the event of non-prosecution. And likewise in the event that settlement takes place by way of abandonment.
If the insurer is bound to pay for a loss or damage the liability for which falls upon a third party, he may exercise the rights of the insured whom he has indemnified and bring his actions.
The insured is entitled in the following cases to claim payment of the full indemnity in return for the transfer of the rights which he holds in the insured thing to the insurance company.

The insured vessel may not be abandoned except in the following cases:

Lack of news, disappearance, total destruction, unseaworthiness due to a fortuitous maritime casualty provided that the matter involves a peril covered by the insurance. And in the event that the insurance covers war risks: capture of the vessel or its detention by order of the authority.

Lack of news after four months enables the abandonment of all steam vessels, and after six months enables the abandonment of all sailing vessels other than those crossing Cape Horn and the Cape of Good Hope, and after eight months enables the abandonment of these latter vessels. The time limits shall run from the date of receipt of the last news.

If the insurance is contracted for a fixed time and its risks were running on the date of dispatch of the last news, the loss of the vessel shall be presumed to have occurred within the time of the insurance.
A vessel shall be unseaworthy if the total cost of repairs required by losses resulting from a maritime peril exceeds three-quarters of the agreed value.

A vessel condemned to be laid up due to its lack of material means of repair shall also be deemed unseaworthy and may be abandoned to the insurers, provided that it is proved that it is unable to sail safely even after being lightened or towed to another port where it would find the necessary means, and provided that it is proved that the shipowners were unable to deliver the necessary spare parts to the place of anchorage.

Conversely, a vessel may neither be deemed unseaworthy nor be abandoned to the insurers if it is condemned to remain idle solely due to its lack of the funds necessary to pay for the expenses of repair and other expenses.

The insured goods may not be abandoned except in the following cases, provided that the matter involves a peril covered by the insurance:

1) In the event of lack of news after the expiry of the time limits prescribed in Article 364.

2) In the event of unfitness of the vessel for the voyage due to a maritime peril, if it is impossible to forward the goods after the expiry of the time limits specified below, and at least if their loading on board another vessel has not commenced within the same time limits:

- Four months if the casualty occurred on the coasts of Europe or its islands, or on the coast of Asia and Africa bordering the Mediterranean Sea, or on the coast of Asia bordering the Black Sea, or on the coasts of the Atlantic Ocean or its islands outside Europe

- Six months if the casualty occurred on other coasts or islands.

These time limits shall run from the day the insured notifies the insurer of the state of unseaworthiness. If the casualty occurred in a place where navigation was interrupted by ice or by force majeure, the time limit shall be extended by the duration of this interruption.

3) If the goods are sold during the voyage as a result of material damage borne by the insurer.

4) If the loss of the goods or the material damage sustained by them reaches at least three-quarters of the insured value, regardless of all other expenses of whatever kind. And in the event that the insurance covers war risks .

5) If the vessel is captured.

6) If it is condemned to remain idle by order of the authority or if it is seized by pirates.

Article 369: If the unseaworthiness of the vessel is declared, the risks of the goods shall remain borne by their insurer until their arrival at the place of destination, and the insurer shall furthermore bear the expenses of unloading, storing and reloading these goods, as well as the increase in freight resulting from their re-forwarding and all salvage expenses relating thereto.

The freight of the vessel may not be abandoned except:

1) If this freight is totally lost by a maritime peril.

2) If news is lacking after the expiry of the time limits specified in Article 364.

3) If the vessel is captured, in the event that the insurance covers war risks .

The right to any action seeking abandonment shall lapse by prescription if it is not exercised within a time limit of six months commencing: from the day of receipt of the news in the event of abandonment due to total loss or due to capture or detention by order of the authority, and from the day of expiry of the time limits specified by Article 364 in the event of abandonment due to lack of news.

And from the day of expiry of the time limits specified in Article 368 in the event of abandonment of the goods due to the unseaworthiness of the vessel.

And in all other cases, from the day on which the insured was enabled to avail himself of his right of abandonment.

In the event of reinsurance, the reinsured insurers must notify the abandonment to the reinsurer within a time limit of one month commencing from the day of notification of the abandonment made by the original insured.

Upon proceeding with the abandonment, the insured must declare all insurances and bottomry loans contracted. The time limit for payment shall be suspended until this declaration is notified, without resulting in any extension of the time limit specified for bringing the action for abandonment in Article 371 If the insured makes a false declaration in bad faith, he shall be deprived of the benefits of the insurance. And upon the occurrence of the maritime average, its settlement shall take place as set out above.

The insurers of the vessel shall not be entitled to its saved freight nor to the claims resulting from the maritime voyage. However, all claims representing a part of the value of the insured things must be abandoned.
Abandonment may neither be partial nor subject to a condition. It shall only cover the insured things exposed to the risk.
The transfer of ownership resulting from the abandonment shall be final and irrevocable. It cannot be affected by any subsequent event, such as the return of the vessel to the port.
Abandonment shall be possible in the event of salvage of the vessel after sinking or stranding.
If the notified abandonment is accepted or deemed valid, the insurer shall be the owner of the insured items starting from the time the casualty occurred.
If the time of payment is not specified in the contract, the insurer shall be obliged to pay the insurance three months after the notification of the abandonment.

All actions arising out of the insurance contract, except for actions for which the law prescribes a shorter period, shall lapse by prescription two years after the due date of the debt, unless the plaintiff proves that it was impossible for him to bring the action.
The modalities of implementation of this Law shall be determined by decree.

Articles 1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 11, 13 and 19 of the Law implemented by Decree No. 11614 dated 04/01/1969 "Acquisition of Real Property Rights in Lebanon by Non-Lebanese" are hereby repealed and replaced by the following:

- New Article 1: No non-Lebanese person, whether natural or legal, nor any Lebanese legal person deemed by this Law to be on the same footing as a foreigner, may acquire by contract or any other legal act inter vivos, any real property right in Lebanese territory or any other real right among the rights designated by this Law except after obtaining a licence granted by a decree adopted by the Council of Ministers upon the proposal of the Minister of Finance. No exception shall be made to this rule save in the cases expressly provided for in this Law or in a special text. No real right of any kind whatsoever may be owned by any person who does not hold a nationality issued by a recognised State or by any person if the ownership conflicts with the provisions of the Constitution regarding the rejection of permanent settlement.

- New Article 3: Subject to the provisions of the new Article (1), the following are excepted and exempted from the licence.

1- Ownership by non-Lebanese natural and legal persons, or those deemed to be on the same footing as non-Lebanese, of built real properties or real properties designated for construction whose area across the entirety of Lebanese territory does not exceed three thousand square metres.

2- Acquisition of real property rights pursuant to the provisions of Articles 33 and 40 of Law No. 58 dated 06/06/1991 "The Expropriation Law".

3- Acquisition of real property rights in implementation of special laws that require their acquisition by way of security or permit it for another reason, and within the limits imposed by such laws and the conditions designated thereby.

4- Acquisition of the following real rights:

a- The right of inheritance for heirs.

b- The right arising from a bequest or a gift concluded between non-Lebanese who fall among their heirs upon their death, and in particular ascendants, descendants and spouses.

c- The rights arising from contracts of usufruct, antichresis, sale with right of redemption (vente à réméré) or for exploitation, mortgage and lease provided for in Decision No. 12 issued on 16/01/1934. (Emphyteutic lease regime Bail emphyteotique), provided that the provisions of the Fourth and Fifth Articles are observed in the acquisition of these rights.

- New Article 5: Antichresis or sale with right of redemption or for exploitation in which a period for exploitation exceeding ten years is specified shall be subject to a licence for its acquisition. As for a mortgage or a privilege, it does not require a licence. However, a non-Lebanese creditor of a debt arising from an antichresis, sale with right of redemption or for exploitation, mortgage or privilege shall not be entitled to purchase the real right by mutual consent or by auction through the judiciary without a prior licence unless no Lebanese bidder comes forward to purchase it at the reserve price fixed for the first auction or at a price exceeding the secured debt and its accessories. In this case, the non-Lebanese creditor shall be entitled to purchase that right by auction, provided that his purchase is made conditional upon selling it to a Lebanese within a time-limit not exceeding two years from the date the award decision becomes final, under penalty of selling this right in accordance with the procedures set forth in the new Article (11): if the creditor is a bank, the provisions of Article 154 of the Code of Money and Credit shall apply to its purchase.

- New Article 7:
